claim: Human nonmuscle myosin-2C is one of the slowest myosins-2 characterized.
source: Nonmuscle myosin-2C, the gene product of MYH14, is one of the slowest myosins-2 as its steady-state ATPase activity lacks potent F-actin activation (Heissler and Manstein, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this in the Introduction section and cites a previous study (Heissler and Manstein, 2011) as support.

claim: The steady-state ATPase activity of nonmuscle myosin-2C lacks potent F-actin activation.
source: Nonmuscle myosin-2C, the gene product of MYH14, is one of the slowest myosins-2 as its steady-state ATPase activity lacks potent F-actin activation (Heissler and Manstein, 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Heissler and Manstein, 2011.

claim: The crystal structure of human nonmuscle myosin-2C motor domain in the pre-powerstroke state was determined at 2.25 Å resolution.
source: To understand how structural adaptations lead to characteristic kinetic features, we solved the 2.25 Å crystal structure of the human nonmuscle myosin-2C motor domain (NM2C) (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution of the crystal structure in the Introduction and Results sections, with supporting data in Table 1.

claim: NM2C was crystallized in the presence of the ATP analog ADP⋅VO4.
source: Crystallization in the presence of the ATP analog ADP⋅VO4 was achieved after truncation of the flexible N-terminal 45 residues extension and the fusion of the NM2C C-terminus to Dictyostelium α-actinin tandem repeats 1 and 2 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the crystallization conditions in the Results section.

claim: The NM2C Cα atoms superimpose with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.57 Å to chicken smooth muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1BR2).
source: The NM2C Cα atoms superimpose with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.57 Å, 0.78 Å, and 0.73 Å to the closely related motor domain structures from chicken smooth muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1BR2), scallop striated muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1QVI), and Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 2XEL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) in the pre-powerstroke state.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific r.m.s.d. values from structural comparison in the Results section.

claim: The NM2C Cα atoms superimpose with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.78 Å to scallop striated muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1QVI).
source: The NM2C Cα atoms superimpose with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.57 Å, 0.78 Å, and 0.73 Å to the closely related motor domain structures from chicken smooth muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1BR2), scallop striated muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1QVI), and Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 2XEL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) in the pre-powerstroke state.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific r.m.s.d. values from structural comparison in the Results section.

claim: The NM2C Cα atoms superimpose with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.73 Å to Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 2XEL).
source: The NM2C Cα atoms superimpose with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.57 Å, 0.78 Å, and 0.73 Å to the closely related motor domain structures from chicken smooth muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1BR2), scallop striated muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1QVI), and Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 2XEL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) in the pre-powerstroke state.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific r.m.s.d. values from structural comparison in the Results section.

claim: In the NM2C pre-powerstroke state, the characteristic salt bridge between switch-1 R261 and switch-2 E483 is formed.
source: NM2C pre-powerstroke state characteristics include a closed conformation of the nucleotide-binding motifs switch-1 and −2 in the active site (Figure 1B). In this conformation, the characteristic salt bridge between switch-1 R261 and switch-2 E483 that is pivotal for the hydrolysis of ATP is formed (Rayment et al., 1993; Furch et al., 1999; Reubold et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this structural feature in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The salt bridge between switch-1 R261 and switch-2 E483 is pivotal for the hydrolysis of ATP.
source: In this conformation, the characteristic salt bridge between switch-1 R261 and switch-2 E483 that is pivotal for the hydrolysis of ATP is formed (Rayment et al., 1993; Furch et al., 1999; Reubold et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript states this functional importance with supporting citations.

claim: A slight reduction in the JK-loop length in NM2C causes an 8.8 Å shift between switch-1 and the U50 kDa.
source: A slight reduction in the JK-loop length in NM2C causes an 8.8 Å shift between switch-1 and the U50 kDa and abolishes the formation of a tight interaction network with residues of the active site found in other class-2 myosins (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific distance measurements from structural analysis.

claim: The reduction in JK-loop length abolishes the formation of a tight interaction network with residues of the active site found in other class-2 myosins.
source: A slight reduction in the JK-loop length in NM2C causes an 8.8 Å shift between switch-1 and the U50 kDa and abolishes the formation of a tight interaction network with residues of the active site found in other class-2 myosins (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: The manuscript describes this structural consequence based on comparative structural analysis.

claim: The active site volume increases 4.3-fold from 697 Å3 in scallop striated muscle myosin-2 to 3054 Å3 for NM2C.
source: Changes in the spheres that describe the active site volumes indicate a 4.3-fold increase from 697 Å3 in the case of scallop striated muscle myosin-2 (PDB entry 1QVI) to 3054 Å3 for NM2C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific volume calculations from structural analysis.

claim: The enlarged accessibility of the active site region observed in the NM2C pre-powerstroke state structure resembles the conformation of the active site found in the actin-bound NM2C rigor state (PDB entry 5J1H).
source: Strikingly, the enlarged accessibility of the active site region observed in the NM2C pre-powerstroke state structure resembles the conformation of the active site found in the actin-bound NM2C rigor state (PDB entry 5J1H), indicating that F-actin binding does not induce major structural rearrangements in the vicinity of the active site (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript compares the pre-powerstroke and rigor state structures.

claim: F-actin binding does not induce major structural rearrangements in the vicinity of the NM2C active site.
source: Strikingly, the enlarged accessibility of the active site region observed in the NM2C pre-powerstroke state structure resembles the conformation of the active site found in the actin-bound NM2C rigor state (PDB entry 5J1H), indicating that F-actin binding does not induce major structural rearrangements in the vicinity of the active site (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from structural comparison between pre-powerstroke and rigor states.

claim: Residue R788 at the interface of converter, Nter, and lever is highly conserved in nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosins-2.
source: Residue R788 at the interface of converter, Nter, and lever is highly conserved in nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosins-2 and the only connecting hub between structural elements of the L50 kDa and the Nter in NM2C (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript states this based on sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: R788 is the only connecting hub between structural elements of the L50 kDa and the Nter in NM2C.
source: Residue R788 at the interface of converter, Nter, and lever is highly conserved in nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosins-2 and the only connecting hub between structural elements of the L50 kDa and the Nter in NM2C (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript identifies this structural feature from the crystal structure.

claim: In NM2C, R788 forms three main chain and five side chain interactions with residues of the SH1-SH2 helix, the converter, and the lever in the pre-powerstroke state.
source: In NM2C, R788 forms three main chain and five side chain interactions with residues of the SH1-SH2 helix, the converter, and the lever in the pre-powerstroke state in addition to a side chain interaction with a water molecule (2.8 Å).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific interactions observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The guanidinium group of R788 forms hydrogen bonds with the main chain carbonyls of residues Q730 and G731 of the SH1 helix.
source: Specifically, the guanidinium group of the R788 side chain of NM2C forms hydrogen bonds with the main chain carbonyls of residues Q730 and G731 of the SH1 helix.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific interaction details from the crystal structure.

claim: The R788E mutation decreases the second-order ATP-binding rate constant K1k+2 five-fold compared to NM2C.
source: Linear fits to the data result in second-order binding rate constants of K1k+2 = 0.48±0.01 µM−1s−1 for NM2C (green), a two-fold reduced ATP binding constant K1k+2 = 0.22±0.01 µM−1s−1 for R788K (yellow), and a five-fold reduced binding rate constant of K1k+2 = 0.09±0.005 µM−1s−1 for R788E (grey) compared to NM2C.
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements comparing NM2C and R788E mutant.

claim: The R788K mutation decreases the second-order ATP-binding rate constant K1k+2 two-fold compared to NM2C.
source: Linear fits to the data result in second-order binding rate constants of K1k+2 = 0.48±0.01 µM−1s−1 for NM2C (green), a two-fold reduced ATP binding constant K1k+2 = 0.22±0.01 µM−1s−1 for R788K (yellow), and a five-fold reduced binding rate constant of K1k+2 = 0.09±0.005 µM−1s−1 for R788E (grey) compared to NM2C.
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements comparing NM2C and R788K mutant.

claim: Nonmuscle myosin-2 specific transient kinetic signatures such as a high k+AD/K1k+2 ratio are absent in R788E.
source: Most importantly, nonmuscle myosin-2 specific transient kinetic signatures such as a high k+AD/K1k+2 ratio (k+AD/K1k+2 ~ 2–20) are absent in R788E (k+AD/K1k+2 ~ 0.02) (Table 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements and compares them to literature values.

claim: The actin-activated ADP release rate k-AD is 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C.
source: Actin-activation of the ADP release (k-AD = 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C, k-AD = 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K, and k-AD = 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E) results in a kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D of ~3.8 for R788E, whereas neutral or negative kinetic coupling are features of NM2C (k-AD/k-D ~ 0.7), R788K (k-AD/k-D ~ 1.1), and other human nonmuscle myosins-2 (Table 4) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements from stopped-flow experiments.

claim: The actin-activated ADP release rate k-AD is 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K.
source: Actin-activation of the ADP release (k-AD = 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C, k-AD = 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K, and k-AD = 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E) results in a kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D of ~3.8 for R788E, whereas neutral or negative kinetic coupling are features of NM2C (k-AD/k-D ~ 0.7), R788K (k-AD/k-D ~ 1.1), and other human nonmuscle myosins-2 (Table 4) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements from stopped-flow experiments.

claim: The actin-activated ADP release rate k-AD is 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E.
source: Actin-activation of the ADP release (k-AD = 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C, k-AD = 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K, and k-AD = 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E) results in a kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D of ~3.8 for R788E, whereas neutral or negative kinetic coupling are features of NM2C (k-AD/k-D ~ 0.7), R788K (k-AD/k-D ~ 1.1), and other human nonmuscle myosins-2 (Table 4) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements from stopped-flow experiments.

claim: The ADP dissociation equilibrium constant KAD increases 10-fold from ~0.26 µM for NM2C to ~3 µM for R788E.
source: The changes in ADP binding and release kinetics of R788E result in a 10-fold increase in the ADP dissociation equilibrium constant KAD (KAD ~0.26 µM for NM2C and ~3 µM for R788E).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated equilibrium constants from kinetic measurements.

claim: The thermodynamic coupling (KAD/KD) for R788E is 42-times stronger than for NM2C.
source: The thermodynamic coupling (KAD/KD = 5) for R788E is 42-times stronger than for NM2C (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated coupling ratios from kinetic measurements.

claim: R788E displays an extraordinarily slow ADP binding rate constant (k+AD = 0.03 ± 0.001 µM−1s−1) in the presence of F-actin.
source: R788E displays an extraordinary slow ADP binding rate constant (k+AD = 0.03 ± 0.001 µM−1s−1) (Table 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) in the presence of F-actin, whereas the kinetic constants for the interaction between actomyosin and ATP, K1k+2, k+2, and 1/K1 are only marginally affected when compared to NM2C (2).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements from stopped-flow experiments.

claim: F-actin can activate the steady-state ATPase activity of R788E to approximately half the kcat of NM2C.
source: F-actin can activate the steady-state ATPase activity of R788E to approximately half the kcat of NM2C (kcat = 0.2 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E and kcat = 0.37 ± 0.02 s−1 of NM2C) (Table 3) under steady-state conditions.
evidence: The manuscript reports steady-state ATPase measurements.

claim: The duty ratio at an F-actin concentration of 190 µM and saturating [ATP] increases from ~0.3 for NM2C and R788K to ~1 for R788E.
source: The duty ratio at an F-actin concentration of 190 µM and saturating [ATP] increases from ~0.3 for NM2C and R788K to ~1 for R788E due to the decreased kcat and the decreased actin-activated ADP release rate k-AD.
evidence: The manuscript calculates duty ratios from kinetic measurements.

claim: R788E does not exhibit a nucleotide-induced change in its intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence signal.
source: The slow nucleotide binding and release kinetics of R788E suggest that the R788-mediated interaction at the converter/Nter/lever interface is allosterically communicated to the active site. This is in line with the observation that R788E does not show a nucleotide-induced change in the intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence signal during steady-state fluorescence measurements and transient-state kinetic assays (Figure 5D,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports fluorescence measurements comparing NM2C and R788E.

claim: The fluorescence change observed with NM2C is attributed to a conformation-induced change in the microenvironment of the conserved relay loop W525.
source: The fluorescence change observed with NM2C is attributed to a conformation-induced change in the microenvironment of the conserved relay loop W525, which is in van der Waals distance to R788.
evidence: The manuscript interprets fluorescence data based on structural information and literature.

claim: W525 is generally regarded as a direct indicator for the switch-2 induced converter rotation.
source: W525 is generally regarded as a direct indicator for the switch-2 induced converter rotation (Malnasi-Csizmadia et al., 2001; Batra and Manstein, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature establishing this relationship.

claim: MD simulations show that the relay helix straightens in NM2C with a steady increase in the angle from approximately 145° to 150°.
source: The relay helix straightens in NM2C with a steady increase in the angle of the relay helix from approximately 145° to 150°, while the angle does not change significantly in R788E and fluctuates around 145° throughout the 100 ns time course of the simulation.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In R788E MD simulations, the relay helix angle does not change significantly and fluctuates around 145° throughout the 100 ns simulation.
source: The relay helix straightens in NM2C with a steady increase in the angle of the relay helix from approximately 145° to 150°, while the angle does not change significantly in R788E and fluctuates around 145° throughout the 100 ns time course of the simulation.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: After 100 ns of MD simulation, the position of the converter and the adjacent lever show an orientation between the post-rigor and pre-powerstroke state in NM2C.
source: After 100 ns, the position of the converter and the adjacent lever show an orientation between the post-rigor and pre-powerstroke state, as compared to the crystal structures of Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 motor domain (PDB entries 1FMW, 2XEL) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations and compares to crystal structures.

claim: The converter undergoes a 27° rotation during MD simulations of NM2C.
source: Likewise, the converter undergoes a 27° rotation that directs lever arm motion (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The indole ring of relay loop W525 changes its conformation by 70–80° during MD simulations of NM2C.
source: With the movement of the relay helix, the indole ring of relay loop W525 changes its conformation by 70–80°, which agrees with the experimentally observed nucleotide-induced change in the intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence signal in NM2C (Figure 5B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations and relates them to experimental observations.

claim: MD simulations for R788E indicate that all interdomain interactions between R788E of the converter and the SH1 helix are lost.
source: MD simulations for R788E indicate that all interdomain interactions between R788E of the converter and the SH1 helix are lost (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In R788E MD simulations, the straightening angle of the relay helix remains constant and abolishes a detectable converter rotation.
source: The straightening angle of the relay helix remains constant and abolishes a detectable converter rotation (Figure 5A,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The salt bridge between switch-2 E483 and switch-1 R261 appears less stable in the MD simulations of R788E compared to NM2C.
source: As a consequence, the salt bridge between switch-2 E483 and switch-1 R261 appears less stable in the MD simulations of R788E as compared to NM2C (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The side chain of relay loop W525 does not undergo a conformational change throughout the time course of the simulation for R788E.
source: The side chain of relay loop W525 does not undergo a conformational change throughout the time course of the simulation for R788E, supporting our experimental observation that mutant construct R788E does not exhibit a nucleotide-induced change in its intrinsic tryptophan fluorescence signal (Figure 5D,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from molecular dynamics simulations and relates them to experimental observations.

claim: R788 is a distant allosteric modulator of switch-2 dynamics at the active site that impacts nucleotide binding and release kinetics in the actin-detached states.
source: In summary, our in silico and experimental in vitro data show that R788 is a distant allosteric modulator of switch-2 dynamics at the active site that impacts nucleotide binding and release kinetics in the actin-detached states.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from MD simulations and kinetic experiments.

claim: R788 acts as a quencher of W525 fluorescence.
source: Moreover, our data support a model of R788 as a quencher of W525 fluorescence (Figure 5D,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model based on fluorescence measurements and MD simulations.

claim: Disruption of the allosteric communication pathway by mutation of R788 abolishes nonmuscle myosin-2 specific kinetic signatures.
source: Disruption of this pathway by mutation of hub residue R788, which forms the center of a cluster of interactions connecting the converter, the SH1-SH2 helix, the relay helix, and the lever, abolishes nonmuscle myosin-2 specific kinetic signatures.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion in the Abstract based on kinetic measurements.

claim: The allosteric communication pathway connects the distal end of the motor domain with the active site.
source: In combination with integrated mutagenesis, ensemble-solution kinetics, and molecular dynamics simulation approaches, the structure reveals an allosteric communication pathway that connects the distal end of the motor domain with the active site.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the Abstract based on structural and kinetic data.

claim: Nonmuscle myosin-2C is essential for the structural integrity of the cytoplasmic architecture during cell shape remodeling and motile events of eukaryotic cells.
source: Nonmuscle myosin-2s are essential for the structural integrity of the cytoplasmic architecture during cell shape remodeling and motile events of eukaryotic cells, whereas all other myosins-2 play eminent roles in the contraction of smooth, cardiac and striated muscle cells (Sellers, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript states this in Figure 1 legend with citation to Sellers, 2000.

claim: Transient kinetic signatures of the nonmuscle myosin-2C enzymatic cycle include a high affinity for ADP.
source: Transient kinetic signatures of the nonmuscle myosin-2C enzymatic cycle include a high affinity for ADP, small kinetic (k-AD/k-D) and thermodynamic (KAD/KD) coupling ratios, and a higher duty ratio than it is commonly found in myosins-2 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Introduction with references to previous work.

claim: Transient kinetic signatures of the nonmuscle myosin-2C enzymatic cycle include small kinetic (k-AD/k-D) and thermodynamic (KAD/KD) coupling ratios.
source: Transient kinetic signatures of the nonmuscle myosin-2C enzymatic cycle include a high affinity for ADP, small kinetic (k-AD/k-D) and thermodynamic (KAD/KD) coupling ratios, and a higher duty ratio than it is commonly found in myosins-2 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Introduction with references to previous work.

claim: Nonmuscle myosin-2C has a higher duty ratio than is commonly found in myosins-2.
source: Transient kinetic signatures of the nonmuscle myosin-2C enzymatic cycle include a high affinity for ADP, small kinetic (k-AD/k-D) and thermodynamic (KAD/KD) coupling ratios, and a higher duty ratio than it is commonly found in myosins-2 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Introduction with references to previous work.

claim: Nonmuscle myosin-2C participates in the active regulation of cytoplasmic contractility in cellular processes including cytokinesis, neuronal dynamics, adhesion, and tension maintenance.
source: The participation in the active regulation of cytoplasmic contractility in cellular processes including cytokinesis, neuronal dynamics, adhesion, and tension maintenance are in line with this interpretation (Takaoka et al., 2014; Wylie and Chantler, 2008; Ebrahim et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The near atomic resolution cryo electron microscopic structure of nonmuscle myosin-2C motor domain bound to F-actin has been determined.
source: Nonmuscle myosin-2C has recently received great attention as the near atomic resolution cryo electron microscopic structure of its motor domain bound to F-actin has been determined (von der Ecken et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites this previous structural work.

claim: The JK-loop constitutes a major connection between switch-1 and the nucleotide.
source: The JK-loop constitutes a major connection between switch-1 and the nucleotide is of great functional significance as a hotspot for human cardiomyopathy-causing mutations in cardiac myosin-2 and the site of exon 7 in Drosophila muscle myosin-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Miller et al., 2007; Van Driest et al., 2004; Havndrup et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript states this with supporting citations to disease-related studies.

claim: The JK-loop is a hotspot for human cardiomyopathy-causing mutations in cardiac myosin-2.
source: The JK-loop constitutes a major connection between switch-1 and the nucleotide is of great functional significance as a hotspot for human cardiomyopathy-causing mutations in cardiac myosin-2 and the site of exon 7 in Drosophila muscle myosin-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Miller et al., 2007; Van Driest et al., 2004; Havndrup et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies identifying disease-causing mutations.

claim: In scallop striated muscle myosin-2, A-loop residue R128 coordinates the interaction to the ADP adenosine in the active site.
source: A-loop residue R128 is coordinating the interaction to the ADP adenosine in the active site of striated muscle myosin-2. The distance between the residues is 3.2 Å.
evidence: The manuscript describes this interaction from structural comparison.

claim: In scallop striated muscle myosin-2, A-loop R128 forms a hydrogen bond (2.8 Å) with E184 of the P-loop.
source: R128 further forms a hydrogen bond (2.8 Å) with E184 of the P-loop.
evidence: The manuscript describes this interaction from structural comparison.

claim: In scallop striated muscle myosin-2, JK-loop N321 is in hydrogen bond interaction with switch-1 N238.
source: JK-loop N321 is in hydrogen bond interaction with switch-1 N238, located at a distance of 4.6 Å to the hydroxyl group of the C2' of the ADP ribose.
evidence: The manuscript describes this interaction from structural comparison.

claim: NM2C lacks all interactions described for scallop striated muscle myosin-2 due to the replacement of R128 with Q150 and JK-loop shortening.
source: Strikingly, NM2C lacks all interactions described for scallop striated muscle myosin-2 due to the replacement of R128 with Q150 and JK-loop shortening.
evidence: The manuscript compares structural features between NM2C and scallop myosin.

claim: The replacement of R128 with Q150 and JK-loop shortening increase the distance to the adenosine in the active site to 5.8 Å in NM2C.
source: Both structural alterations increase the distance to the adenosine in the active site to 5.8 Å and disrupt constrains between swich-1 and the JK-loop (Figure 2B,C,E).
evidence: The manuscript provides distance measurements from structural analysis.

claim: The NM2C JK-loop is highly flexible despite its reduced length.
source: The temperature factors obtained from the refined crystal structure show that the NM2C JK-loop is highly flexible despite its reduced length.
evidence: The manuscript reports B-factors from the crystal structure refinement.

claim: The flexibility of the NM2C JK-loop is attributed to the lack of constraints with switch-1 residues and the bound nucleotide.
source: We attribute the flexibility to the lack of constraints with switch-1 residues and the bound nucleotide (Figure 2A,B,C,E).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from structural analysis and B-factor data.

claim: The replacement of an arginine with K255 and a glutamate with H700 in NM2C is expected to weaken a tight and highly conserved interaction network between the active site and the Nter.
source: Further, the substitution of an arginine with K255 and a glutamate with H700 in NM2C is expected to weaken a tight and highly conserved interaction network between the active site and the Nter of NM2C (Table 2) (Risal et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript predicts this effect based on structural comparison and literature.

claim: The interconnectivity of the highly conserved nucleotide switches and myosin subdomains is weaker in NM2C compared to fast sarcomeric myosins-2.
source: In summary, our comparative structural analysis of the active site of myosins-2 suggests that the interconnectivity of the highly conserved nucleotide switches and myosin subdomains is weaker in NM2C and likely other nonmuscle myosins-2 compared to fast sarcomeric myosins-2.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from comparative structural analysis.

claim: Replacement of R788 with a lysine in muscle myosins-2 weakens the interaction between the converter, Nter, and lever in all states of the myosin and actomyosin kinetic cycle.
source: Notably, replacement of R788 with a lysine in muscle myosins-2 weakens the interaction between the aforementioned structural elements in all states of the myosin and actomyosin kinetic cycle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from structural comparison between NM2C and muscle myosins.

claim: The R788 side chain:main chain interaction is evident in crystal structures of nonmuscle myosins-2 in the nucleotide-free (PDB entry 4PD3) and the phosphate-release state (PDB entry 4PJK).
source: Notably, the R788 side chain:main chain interaction is also evident in crystal structures of nonmuscle myosins-2 in the nucleotide-free (PDB entry 4PD3) and the phosphate-release state (PDB entry 4PJK) (not shown).
evidence: The manuscript compares the NM2C structure to other published structures.

claim: The tight interaction network formed by R788 is required for the precise positioning and coupling of the converter, the SH1-SH2 helix, the relay helix, and the lever arm throughout all steps of the myosin ATPase cycle.
source: We therefore hypothesize that (i) the tight interaction network formed by R788 is required for the precise positioning and coupling of the converter, the SH1-SH2 helix, the relay helix, and the lever arm throughout all steps of the myosin ATPase cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and that (ii) different communication pathways between the active site and the distal end of the motor domain are employed by NM2C in the presence and absence of F-actin.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: Different communication pathways between the active site and the distal end of the motor domain are employed by NM2C in the presence and absence of F-actin.
source: We therefore hypothesize that (i) the tight interaction network formed by R788 is required for the precise positioning and coupling of the converter, the SH1-SH2 helix, the relay helix, and the lever arm throughout all steps of the myosin ATPase cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and that (ii) different communication pathways between the active site and the distal end of the motor domain are employed by NM2C in the presence and absence of F-actin.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on structural and kinetic analysis.

claim: Transient kinetic changes in R788E are more severe than in R788K and mainly affect nucleotide binding and release kinetics.
source: Confirming our hypotheses, transient kinetic changes in R788E are more severe than in R788K and mainly affect nucleotide binding and release kinetics (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements comparing the mutants.

claim: Transient kinetic changes are more pronounced in the absence of F-actin, as seen in single-turnover measurements.
source: Transient kinetic changes are more pronounced in the absence of F-actin, as seen in single-turnover measurements (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements under different conditions.

claim: The kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D is ~3.8 for R788E.
source: Actin-activation of the ADP release (k-AD = 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C, k-AD = 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K, and k-AD = 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E) results in a kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D of ~3.8 for R788E, whereas neutral or negative kinetic coupling are features of NM2C (k-AD/k-D ~ 0.7), R788K (k-AD/k-D ~ 1.1), and other human nonmuscle myosins-2 (Table 4) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript calculates this ratio from kinetic measurements.

claim: The kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D is ~0.7 for NM2C.
source: Actin-activation of the ADP release (k-AD = 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C, k-AD = 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K, and k-AD = 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E) results in a kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D of ~3.8 for R788E, whereas neutral or negative kinetic coupling are features of NM2C (k-AD/k-D ~ 0.7), R788K (k-AD/k-D ~ 1.1), and other human nonmuscle myosins-2 (Table 4) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript calculates this ratio from kinetic measurements.

claim: The kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D is ~1.1 for R788K.
source: Actin-activation of the ADP release (k-AD = 0.68 ± 0.01 s−1 for NM2C, k-AD = 0.59 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788K, and k-AD = 0.19 ± 0.01 s−1 for R788E) results in a kinetic coupling constant k-AD/k-D of ~3.8 for R788E, whereas neutral or negative kinetic coupling are features of NM2C (k-AD/k-D ~ 0.7), R788K (k-AD/k-D ~ 1.1), and other human nonmuscle myosins-2 (Table 4) (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript calculates this ratio from kinetic measurements.

claim: F-actin affinities are largely unaffected by the R788E mutation.
source: F-actin affinities are largely unaffected by the R788E mutation, which is in line with the observation that switch-1 dynamics are only marginally affected in comparative MD simulations.
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements and relates them to MD simulation results.

claim: ActoNM2C preferentially binds ADP over ATP.
source: The presence of F-actin however establishes ATP/ADP selectivity in the actomyosin ATPase cycle: ActoNM2C preferentially binds ADP over ATP, whereas actoR788E preferentially binds ATP over ADP (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements comparing nucleotide binding rates.

claim: ActoR788E preferentially binds ATP over ADP.
source: The presence of F-actin however establishes ATP/ADP selectivity in the actomyosin ATPase cycle: ActoNM2C preferentially binds ADP over ATP, whereas actoR788E preferentially binds ATP over ADP (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements comparing nucleotide binding rates.

claim: ATP/ADP selectivity is established by actin-induced conformational changes in the myosin motor domain.
source: ATP/ADP selectivity is established by actin-induced conformational changes in the myosin motor domain and underlines that the coupling mechanism from the active site to the converter and vice versa is different in the presence and absence of F-actin.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from kinetic data showing different selectivity in presence and absence of actin.

claim: The coupling mechanism from the active site to the converter is different in the presence and absence of F-actin.
source: ATP/ADP selectivity is established by actin-induced conformational changes in the myosin motor domain and underlines that the coupling mechanism from the active site to the converter and vice versa is different in the presence and absence of F-actin.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from kinetic data and relates it to literature.

claim: Distinct pathways exist for the myosin and actin-activated ATPase cycle.
source: This observation is in line with recent reports on distinct pathways for the myosin and actin-activated ATPase cycle (Llinas et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent literature supporting this conclusion.

claim: Nonmuscle myosin-2C assembles into small bipolar filaments that dynamically tether actin filaments in cells.
source: Nonmuscle myosin-2C assembles into small bipolar filaments that dynamically tether actin filaments in cells (Ebrahim et al., 2013; Billington et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on NM2C filament assembly and function.

claim: The calculated duty ratio of NM2C suggests that ~14 motor domains would be needed to be geometrically capable of interacting with F-actin at any given time.
source: Based on our kinetic data, the calculated duty ratio of NM2C suggests that ~14 motor domains would be needed to be geometrically capable of interacting with F-actin at any given time.
evidence: The manuscript calculates this from kinetic measurements.

claim: The number of motor domains needed to interact with F-actin is identical to the number of motor domains per nonmuscle myosin-2C half filament.
source: This number is identical to the number of motor domains per nonmuscle myosin-2C half filament, suggesting that the filament may be at the threshold of being processive in the absence of external loads (Billington et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript compares calculated duty ratio to known filament structure.

claim: Resisting load applied to the lever slows down the actin-activated ADP release from the lead motor of nonmuscle myosin-2A around fivefold.
source: Resisting load applied to the lever slows down the actin-activated ADP release from the lead motor of nonmuscle myosin-2A around fivefold thereby increasing the duty ratio, but does not alter the rate of ATP binding (Hundt et al., 2016; Kovács et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on load-dependent kinetics.

claim: Resisting load applied to the lever increases the duty ratio of nonmuscle myosin-2A but does not alter the rate of ATP binding.
source: Resisting load applied to the lever slows down the actin-activated ADP release from the lead motor of nonmuscle myosin-2A around fivefold thereby increasing the duty ratio, but does not alter the rate of ATP binding (Hundt et al., 2016; Kovács et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on load-dependent kinetics.

claim: The kinetic signatures of the strained nonmuscle myosin-2A lead motor are very similar to the observed kinetic features of R788E.
source: The kinetic signatures of the strained nonmuscle myosin-2A lead motor are very similar to the observed kinetic features of R788E.
evidence: The manuscript compares kinetic data from R788E to literature on load-dependent kinetics.

claim: Internal strain in the nonmuscle myosin-2 dimer distorts the lead motor at the converter/lever interface and leads to its axial translation.
source: We propose that internal strain in the nonmuscle myosin-2 dimer distorts the lead motor at the converter/lever interface and leads to its axial translation as seen in electron microscopic studies (Burgess et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on kinetic data and cites EM studies.

claim: Axial translation of the converter abolishes the interaction of R788 with residues of the SH1-SH2 helix and the relay helix.
source: This translation abolishes the interaction of the converter R788 with residues of the SH1-SH2 helix and the relay helix, thereby uncoupling the myosin subdomains and disrupting the communication pathway from the converter to the active site, which is expected to result in a similar kinetic effect as in R788E.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism to explain load-dependent behavior.

claim: A motor in a nonmuscle myosin-2 filament would decrease its enzymatic activity and stay strongly bound to F-actin under strain.
source: Consequently, a motor in a nonmuscle myosin-2 filament would decrease its enzymatic activity and stay strongly bound to F-actin.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this consequence of the proposed strain-sensing mechanism.

claim: Decreased enzymatic activity and strong F-actin binding under strain is required to generate processivity and cytoskeletal tension.
source: This feature is required to generate processivity and cytoskeletal tension and of physiological significance in the maintenance of cell shape and tensional homeostasis in the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this functional significance based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Missense mutations G376C and R726S are associated with autosomal dominant hearing impairment (DFNA4).
source: Importantly, several key residues involved in the allosteric communication pathway are implicated in the onset and progression of debilitating human diseases (Fu et al., 2016; Donaudy et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2017). Missense mutation G376C is in proximity to residues C324 of helix J and R328 of the JK-loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies linking these mutations to disease.

claim: Missense mutation G376C may interfere with the nucleotide binding and release kinetics from the NM2C active site.
source: Based on its location, we suggest that this substitution may interfere with the nucleotide binding and release kinetics from the NM2C active site.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this effect based on the mutation's location in the structure.

claim: Missense mutation R726S is expected to disrupt the interaction between the SH1-SH2 helix and the Nter.
source: Missense mutation R726S is in the SH1-SH2 helix and the guanidinium group of the wild-type arginine interacts (3.3 Å) with the NM2C Nter. The serine residue is expected to disrupt this interaction because of the shorter side chain and different charge when compared to arginine.
evidence: The manuscript predicts this effect based on structural analysis of the mutation.

claim: Mutations G376C and R726S may impact the interaction of the motor domain with nucleotides, thereby contributing to impaired tension-sensing and maintenance of nonmuscle myosin-2C in the human cochlea.
source: It is therefore likely that these mutations may impact the interaction of the motor domain with nucleotides, thereby contributing to impaired tension-sensing and maintenance of nonmuscle myosin-2C in the human cochlea (Fu et al., 2016; Donaudy et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this disease mechanism based on structural and kinetic analysis.

claim: The reduced number of hydrogen bond interactions between P-loop, switch-1, and the Nter contribute to the low thermodynamic and kinetic coupling efficiency in NM2C.
source: At the active site, the reduced number of hydrogen bond interactions between P-loop, switch-1, and the Nter together with the reduced interconnectivity within the motor domain contribute to the low thermodynamic (KAD/KD) and kinetic (k-AD/k-D) coupling efficiency and the efficiency of F-actin to displace ADP and Pi during the catalytic cycle in NM2C and likely other nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosins-2 compared to cardiac and striated muscle myosins-2 (Table 2) (Risal et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript relates structural features to kinetic properties with supporting citation.

claim: The reduced interconnectivity within the motor domain contributes to the efficiency of F-actin to displace ADP and Pi during the catalytic cycle in NM2C.
source: At the active site, the reduced number of hydrogen bond interactions between P-loop, switch-1, and the Nter together with the reduced interconnectivity within the motor domain contribute to the low thermodynamic (KAD/KD) and kinetic (k-AD/k-D) coupling efficiency and the efficiency of F-actin to displace ADP and Pi during the catalytic cycle in NM2C and likely other nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosins-2 compared to cardiac and striated muscle myosins-2 (Table 2) (Risal et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript relates structural features to kinetic properties with supporting citation.

claim: Partial uncoupling of the communication pathway by the conservative R788K mutation has a moderate impact on nucleotide binding and release kinetics in the myosin ATPase cycle compared to NM2C.
source: Partial uncoupling of the communication pathway by the conservative R788K mutation has a moderate impact on nucleotide binding and release kinetics (Table 3) in the myosin ATPase cycle compared to NM2C.
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements comparing R788K to NM2C.

claim: Complete uncoupling of the converter from the motor domain in R788E slows down all kinetic steps of the myosin ATPase cycle.
source: Complete uncoupling of the converter from the motor domain in R788E slows down all kinetic steps of the myosin ATPase cycle and decreases its actin-activation, due to altered switch-2 dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript reports kinetic measurements and relates them to structural changes.

claim: The observed kinetic phenotype of the R788E myosin ATPase cycle is similar to Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 non-hydrolyzer mutants.
source: The observed kinetic phenotype of the R788E myosin ATPase cycle is similar to the Dictyostelium nonmuscle myosin-2 non-hydrolyzer mutants in which the salt bridge between switch-1 and switch-2 is completely destroyed by mutagenesis and unable to form (Furch et al., 1999; Friedman et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript compares R788E kinetics to literature on non-hydrolyzer mutants.

claim: Non-hydrolyzer mutants are characterized by long-lived ATP states and reduced nucleotide release and binding kinetics, including a drastic decrease in k+AD.
source: Non-hydrolyzer mutants are characterized by long-lived ATP states and reduced nucleotide release and binding kinetics, including a drastic decrease in k+AD (Furch et al., 1999; Friedman et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies characterizing non-hydrolyzer mutants.

claim: Dictyostelium myosin-2 non-hydrolyzer mutants do not exhibit a nucleotide-induced change in the intrinsic fluorescence signal.
source: Like R788E, Dictyostelium myosin-2 non-hydrolyzer mutants do not exhibit a nucleotide-induced change in the intrinsic fluorescence signal (Furch et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on non-hydrolyzer mutants.

claim: The lack of an intrinsic fluorescence signal in R788E is caused by the blockage of the communication pathway on the relay helix before or at Y518.
source: It is of note that the lack of an intrinsic fluorescence signal in R788E is caused by the blockage of the communication pathway on the relay helix before or at Y518 (Figure 6A,B), whereas the impairment of the nucleotide switches to form a salt bridge and the resulting lack of the switch-2-induced conformational change of the relay helix is the expected cause in the non-hydrolyzer mutants.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from structural and kinetic data.

claim: The allosteric coupling pathway may be of significance in intermolecular gating and load-sensitivity of nonmuscle myosins-2.
source: The allosteric coupling pathway may be of significance in intermolecular gating and load-sensitivity of nonmuscle myosins-2 that is important for their physiological function as cytoskeletal strain-sensor in the context of stress fibers, actin arcs, and cortical actin-based structures.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this physiological significance in the Abstract.

claim: The actomyosin interaction and tension exerted by a sarcomeric array of nonmuscle myosin-2C is of importance for the function and organization of the apical junctional complex in the organ of Corti.
source: The actomyosin interaction and hence the tension exerted by a sarcomeric array of nonmuscle myosin-2C is of importance for the function and organization of the apical junctional complex in the organ of Corti and actin-rich structures including stress fibers and actin arcs (Ebrahim et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on NM2C physiological function.
